chapterTitle: Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood, and the Steps of Christ
themeTitle: “You Are a Chosen Race, a Royal Priesthood, a Holy Nation”

scripture.text: Putting away therefore all wickedness, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all evil speaking,
scripture.understanding: ἀποθέμενοι οὖν, “Putting away therefore” — the same verb James used, like taking off dirty clothes (James 1:21). Five things to strip off: κακία, “wickedness” — from the evil family: malice, ill-will; δόλος, “deceit” — bait, trickery; ὑπόκρισις, “hypocrisies” — acting a part; φθόνος, “envies”; καταλαλιά, “evil speaking” — slander, talking people down, as in James 4:11. Every one of them poisons the love commanded in 1:22.

scripture.text: as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow,
scripture.understanding: ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη, “as newborn babies” — ἀρτιγέννητος, from the birth family: just born, following the new birth of 1:23. τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα ἐπιποθήσατε, “long for the pure milk of the Word” — ἐπιποθέω, to crave intensely, as a baby cries for milk. ἄδολος, ‘without deceit’, the opposite of δόλος in verse 1. λογικός can mean ‘rational’ or ‘spiritual’ (Romans 12:1 ‘spiritual service’); the WEB renders it ‘of the Word’, connecting it with the λόγος of 1:23 — the nourishment is God's word. ἵνα ἐν αὐτῷ αὐξηθῆτε, “that with it you may grow” — many manuscripts add ‘to salvation’.

scripture.text: if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious:
scripture.understanding: εἰ ἐγεύσασθε ὅτι χρηστὸς ὁ κύριος, “if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious” — γεύομαι, to taste by experience; χρηστός, from the good family: kind, gracious, good in its kindness, as distinct from ἀγαθός (useful good) and καλός (beautiful good). An echo of Psalm 34:8. Some early Christians heard a wordplay: χρηστός (kind) and Χριστός (Christ).

scripture.text: coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.
scripture.understanding: πρὸς ὃν προσερχόμενοι, “coming to him” — προσέρχομαι, the word for approaching God in worship (Hebrews 4:16). λίθον ζῶντα, “a living stone” — ζάω, from the life family: Christ the risen stone. ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μὲν ἀποδεδοκιμασμένον, “rejected indeed by men” — ἀποδοκιμάζω, from the test family: tested and thrown out as unfit. παρὰ δὲ θεῷ ἐκλεκτὸν ἔντιμον, “but chosen by God, precious” — what the builders discarded, God selected.

scripture.text: You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: καὶ αὐτοὶ ὡς λίθοι ζῶντες, “You also, as living stones” — ζάω, from the life family: alive with Christ's life. Peter, the ‘rock’, calls every believer a living stone. οἰκοδομεῖσθε οἶκος πνευματικός, “are built up as a spiritual house” — a temple made of people. εἰς ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον, “to be a holy priesthood” — ἱεράτευμα, a body of priests. ἀνενέγκαι πνευματικὰς θυσίας, “to offer up spiritual sacrifices” — ἀναφέρω and θυσία, from the offering family: no longer animals, but praise, good works and our own bodies (Hebrews 13:15–16; Romans 12:1). εὐπροσδέκτους, “acceptable,” only διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “through Jesus Christ.”

scripture.text: Because it is contained in Scripture, “Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and precious: He who believes in him will not be disappointed.”
scripture.understanding: “Because it is contained in Scripture, ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and precious’” — from Isaiah 28:16. ἀκρογωνιαῖος, the corner foundation stone that fixes the line of the whole building. ἐκλεκτὸν ἔντιμον, the same two words as verse 4. “He who believes in him will not be disappointed” — καταισχύνω, to put to shame: trust in Him will never leave you embarrassed.

scripture.text: For you who believe therefore is the honor, but for those who are disobedient, “The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone,”
scripture.understanding: ὑμῖν οὖν ἡ τιμή τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, “For you who believe therefore is the honor” — τιμή, the noun of ἔντιμος, ‘precious’: the stone's honour is shared with those who trust it. ἀπειθοῦσιν δέ, “but for those who are disobedient” — ἀπειθέω, refusing to be persuaded. Then Psalm 118:22: “The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone” — ἀποδοκιμάζω again, from the test family; κεφαλὴ γωνίας, ‘head of the corner’. Jesus quoted this psalm about Himself (Matthew 21:42), and Peter quoted it before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:11).

scripture.text: and, “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.” For they stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed.
scripture.understanding: “and, ‘a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.’” — from Isaiah 8:14. πρόσκομμα, something you strike your foot against; πέτρα, a rock — the word Jesus used in Matthew 16:18; σκάνδαλον, the trigger of a trap. The same stone is a foundation for some and a stumbling block for others. οἳ προσκόπτουσιν τῷ λόγῳ ἀπειθοῦντες, “For they stumble at the word, being disobedient” — λόγος, from the word family: they trip over the message by refusing to obey it. εἰς ὃ καὶ ἐτέθησαν, “to which also they were appointed” — what God appointed is that disobedience to the word leads to stumbling; Scripture holds both God's sovereignty and human responsibility here without explaining away either.

scripture.text: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light:
scripture.understanding: ὑμεῖς δὲ γένος ἐκλεκτόν, “But you are a chosen race” — four titles once given to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5–6; Isaiah 43:20–21), now given to the church of Jews and Gentiles. γένος, a family line; βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, “a royal priesthood” — kings and priests together; ἔθνος ἅγιον, “a holy nation”; λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, “a people for God’s own possession” — περιποίησις, a treasure acquired and kept. The purpose: ὅπως τὰς ἀρετὰς ἐξαγγείλητε, “that you may proclaim the excellence” — ἀρετή, the praiseworthy deeds and virtues of God. ἐκ σκότους … εἰς τὸ θαυμαστὸν αὐτοῦ φῶς, “out of darkness into his marvelous light.” σκότος is from the darkness family — darkness as a realm or condition — the opposite of light.

scripture.text: who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.
scripture.understanding: οἵ ποτε οὐ λαός, νῦν δὲ λαὸς θεοῦ, “who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people” — from Hosea 1:10 and 2:23, where God named Hosea's children ‘Not my people’ and ‘Not pitied’, then promised to reverse the names. οἱ οὐκ ἠλεημένοι, νῦν δὲ ἐλεηθέντες, “who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” — ἐλεέω, from the mercy family: mercy that acts. Gentiles who were never God's people are now included.

scripture.text: Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
scripture.understanding: ἀγαπητοί, παρακαλῶ, “Beloved, I beg you” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family. ὡς παροίκους καὶ παρεπιδήμους, “as foreigners and pilgrims” — two words for not belonging: πάροικος, a resident alien, and παρεπίδημος, a temporary visitor, as in 1:1. ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν, “to abstain from fleshly lusts” — σαρκικός, belonging to the fallen nature. αἵτινες στρατεύονται κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς, “which war against the soul” — στρατεύομαι, the same military verb James used for pleasures that ‘war in your members’ (James 4:1). ψυχή, from the life family.

scripture.text: having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they see, glorify God in the day of visitation.
scripture.understanding: τὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἔχοντες καλήν, “having good behavior among the nations” — καλός, from the good family: attractive, beautiful goodness that people can see. ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν ὡς κακοποιῶν, “so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers” — καταλαλέω, to slander; κακοποιός, from the evil family: a wrongdoer, perhaps even a criminal. ἐκ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων ἐποπτεύοντες, “they may by your good works, which they see” — καλὰ ἔργα, the good family and the work family together; ἐποπτεύω, from the see family: to watch closely, as an eyewitness. “glorify God in the day of visitation” — ἡμέρα, from the time family; ἐπισκοπή, God's visit, whether in mercy now or in judgement at the end.

scripture.text: Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme;
scripture.understanding: ὑποτάγητε πάσῃ ἀνθρωπίνῃ κτίσει, “Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man” — ὑποτάσσω, to rank yourself under, the same verb as ‘Be subject … to God’ (James 4:7). κτίσις, a creation, an institution set up by people. διὰ τὸν κύριον, “for the Lord’s sake” — the motive is not fear of the state but loyalty to Christ. “whether to the king, as supreme” — βασιλεύς, the emperor, at this time Nero. ὑπερέχω, to be above.

scripture.text: or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
scripture.understanding: “or to governors, as sent by him” — ἡγεμών, a provincial governor, like Pilate or Felix. Their task: εἰς ἐκδίκησιν κακοποιῶν, “for vengeance on evildoers” — κακοποιός, from the evil family, as in verse 12; ἔπαινον δὲ ἀγαθοποιῶν, “and for praise to those who do well” — ἀγαθοποιός, from the good family: those who do good. Peter describes what government is meant to do (Romans 13:3–4), even when it fails.

scripture.text: For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men:
scripture.understanding: ὅτι οὕτως ἐστὶν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, “For this is the will of God” — θέλημα, what God desires. ἀγαθοποιοῦντας φιμοῦν, “that by well-doing you should put to silence” — ἀγαθοποιέω, from the good family: doing good; φιμόω, to muzzle, as an ox is muzzled. τὴν τῶν ἀφρόνων ἀνθρώπων ἀγνωσίαν, “the ignorance of foolish men” — ἄφρων, senseless; ἀγνωσία, not-knowing. Slander is best answered not by argument but by a good life.

scripture.text: as free, and not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
scripture.understanding: ὡς ἐλεύθεροι, “as free” — ἐλεύθερος: believers are truly free (James 1:25; 2:12). καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐπικάλυμμα ἔχοντες τῆς κακίας τὴν ἐλευθερίαν, “and not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness” — ἐπικάλυμμα, a veil or cover-up; κακία, from the evil family, as in verse 1. Freedom is not a disguise for sin (Galatians 5:13). ἀλλ᾽ ὡς θεοῦ δοῦλοι, “but as bondservants of God” — δοῦλος, from the servant family: wholly owned. True freedom is slavery to God.

scripture.text: Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.
scripture.understanding: Four short commands. πάντας τιμήσατε, “Honor all men” — τιμάω: every person, made in God's image, deserves respect. τὴν ἀδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε, “Love the brotherhood” — ἀγαπάω, from the love family; ἀδελφότης, the whole family of believers. τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε, “Fear God” — φοβέω: reverence is reserved for God alone. τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε, “Honor the king” — the same τιμάω as for all people: the emperor gets honour, but only God gets fear.

scripture.text: Servants, be in subjection to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wicked.
scripture.understanding: οἱ οἰκέται, “Servants” — οἰκέτης, from the servant family: a household slave, a member of the house staff, as distinct from δοῦλος (v. 16), a slave as someone owned. ὑποτασσόμενοι ἐν παντὶ φόβῳ τοῖς δεσπόταις, “be in subjection to your masters with all fear” — δεσπότης, an owner with full authority; φόβος here is reverence towards God (v. 17). οὐ μόνον τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς καὶ ἐπιεικέσιν, “not only to the good and gentle” — ἀγαθός, from the good family; ἐπιεικής, the ‘gentle’ of James 3:17. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σκολιοῖς, “but also to the wicked” — σκολιός, crooked, perverse. Peter addresses slaves directly as responsible people with dignity before God; he regulates the situation they are in without approving of slavery itself.

scripture.text: For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God.
scripture.understanding: τοῦτο γὰρ χάρις, “For it is commendable” — literally ‘this is grace’: favour in God's sight. εἰ διὰ συνείδησιν θεοῦ, “because of conscience toward God” — συνείδησις, awareness of God's presence. ὑποφέρει τις λύπας πάσχων ἀδίκως, “if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly” — ὑποφέρω, to bear up under; λύπη, grief, pain; πάσχω, from the suffer family: to undergo something painful done to you; ἀδίκως, unfairly.

scripture.text: For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.
scripture.understanding: ποῖον γὰρ κλέος, “For what glory is it” — κλέος, fame, credit. εἰ ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ κολαφιζόμενοι ὑπομενεῖτε, “if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating” — ἁμαρτάνω, from the sin family; κολαφίζω, to strike with the fist, the word used of the soldiers striking Jesus (Matthew 26:67); ὑπομένω, from the endurance family: to remain under. ἀλλ᾽ εἰ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καὶ πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε, “But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering” — ἀγαθοποιέω, from the good family, and πάσχω, from the suffer family. τοῦτο χάρις παρὰ θεῷ, “this is commendable with God” — grace again, as in verse 19.

scripture.text: For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps,
scripture.understanding: εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐκλήθητε, “For to this you were called” — καλέω: suffering for doing good is part of the calling. ὅτι καὶ Χριστὸς ἔπαθεν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν, “because Christ also suffered for us” — πάσχω, from the suffer family. ὑμῖν ὑπολιμπάνων ὑπογραμμόν, “leaving you an example” — ὑπογραμμός, from the pattern family: a writing-copy, the line of letters a teacher wrote for a child to trace underneath, as distinct from τύπος (a model) or ὑπόδειγμα (an example to copy). ἵνα ἐπακολουθήσητε τοῖς ἴχνεσιν αὐτοῦ, “that you should follow his steps” — ἴχνος, a footprint. Trace His letters; walk in His footprints.

scripture.text: who did not sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.”
scripture.understanding: ὃς ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἐποίησεν, “who did not sin” — ἁμαρτία, from the sin family. Then Isaiah 53:9: “neither was deceit found in his mouth” — δόλος, the deceit of verse 1. Peter, who lived with Jesus for three years, testifies to His sinlessness. Isaiah 53 runs through verses 22–25.

scripture.text: Who, when he was cursed, didn’t curse back. When he suffered, didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
scripture.understanding: ὃς λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει, “Who, when he was cursed, didn’t curse back” — λοιδορέω, to abuse verbally; ἀντιλοιδορέω, to insult in return. πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει, “When he suffered, didn’t threaten” — πάσχω, from the suffer family. Peter watched it happen at the trials (Matthew 26:63; 27:12–14). παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως, “but committed himself to him who judges righteously” — παραδίδωμι, to hand over: Jesus handed His cause to the Father. That is how to suffer without revenge.

scripture.text: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed.
scripture.understanding: ὃς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον, “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” — ἀναφέρω, from the offering family: the same verb as ‘offer up’ in verse 5, used of carrying a sacrifice up to the altar; ἁμαρτία, from the sin family; ξύλον, wood, the cross, recalling Deuteronomy 21:23. ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν, “that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness” — ζάω, from the life family. οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε, “by whose stripes you were healed” — μώλωψ, the welt left by a whip; ἰάομαι, from the heal family: the physician's word. From Isaiah 53:5. Writing to beaten slaves, Peter points them to the beaten Saviour whose wounds healed the deepest wound, sin.

scripture.text: For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
scripture.understanding: ἦτε γὰρ ὡς πρόβατα πλανώμενοι, “For you were going astray like sheep” — πλανάω, to wander off, the verb Isaiah uses of straying sheep (Isaiah 53:6) and James of the straying believer (James 5:19). ἀλλὰ ἐπεστράφητε νῦν, “but now have returned” — ἐπιστρέφω, to turn back, the word James used for restoring a wanderer (James 5:19–20). ἐπὶ τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, “to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” — ποιμήν, shepherd; ἐπίσκοπος, the one who watches over; ψυχή, from the life family. Peter, told three times to feed Christ's sheep, now points the sheep to the Chief Shepherd (5:4).

visualMeditations.title: The Hungry Newborn
visualMeditations.image: Picture a newborn baby a few hours old. She does not care about comfort, toys or attention; she wants one thing. When she is hungry she cries with her whole body until she is fed — and then, satisfied, she sleeps and grows. Before feeding, her mother gently removes the soiled clothes and wraps her in clean ones.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Putting away therefore all wickedness, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all evil speaking” (v. 1), “as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (v. 2). Spiritual growth needs two things: putting off what poisons and craving what nourishes. If you have “tasted that the Lord is gracious” (v. 3), you will want more. Is your appetite for God's word as strong as a newborn's for milk?

visualMeditations.title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
visualMeditations.image: Picture builders on a great construction site examining stones from the quarry. One stone seems the wrong shape. They test it, frown, and toss it aside onto the rubble heap. Later, when the chief architect arrives, he walks straight to the rubble heap, picks up that very stone and sets it at the corner, where every wall will be measured from it. Then other stones — rough, ordinary, alive — are fitted to it one by one, until a temple rises.
visualMeditations.meaning: “The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone” (v. 7). “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (v. 5). Jesus was rejected by men but chosen by God. Now you are a living stone in His temple. Your life is lined up by Him and joined to others.

visualMeditations.title: Out of Darkness into Light
visualMeditations.image: Picture people stumbling in a deep, dark cave, unable to see their hands, lost and afraid. Then a voice calls their names, a door opens, and they walk out blinking into the brilliant light of morning. Someone places a royal robe on their shoulders and a priest's turban on their heads, and says, ‘You belong to the King.’
visualMeditations.meaning: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (v. 9). You were once ‘no people’; now you are God's people. Your identity is royal and priestly, and your purpose is to declare His excellence.

visualMeditations.title: Tracing the Letters
visualMeditations.image: Picture a child in an ancient schoolroom with a wax tablet. At the top the teacher has written a line of perfect letters. The child presses the stylus into the wax and slowly traces underneath, letter by letter, following every curve. Then picture a man walking ahead on a dusty road, his footprints pressed into the dirt, and others stepping exactly where he stepped.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (v. 21). When He was insulted, He did not insult back; when He suffered, He did not threaten, “but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (v. 23). And “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (v. 24). Christ is both your example to trace and your Saviour who bore what you never could.

structure.label: Grow by the Word (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Put away malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander, and like newborn babies crave the pure milk of the word, so that you grow, since you have tasted that the Lord is good.

structure.label: Living Stones and a Spiritual House (v. 4-8)
structure.body: Come to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, and be built as living stones into a spiritual house and holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices; Scripture calls Him the precious cornerstone for believers and a stone of stumbling for the disobedient.

structure.label: God's Own People (v. 9-10)
structure.body: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation and God's own people, called out of darkness into light to proclaim His excellence; once not a people, now God's people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

structure.label: Good Conduct Among the Nations (v. 11-17)
structure.body: As foreigners, abstain from fleshly desires; live good lives so that slanderers see your good works and glorify God; submit to human authorities for the Lord's sake; silence ignorance by doing good; live as free people who are God's servants; honour all, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the king.

structure.label: Suffering Like Christ (v. 18-25)
structure.body: Servants should submit to masters, even harsh ones, since enduring unjust suffering with a conscience towards God is grace; Christ suffered for us, leaving an example: He did not sin, retaliate or threaten, but entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge; He bore our sins on the tree, and by His wounds we are healed; we were straying sheep, now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls.

sections.heading: Newborns Who Become a Temple
paragraphs: Chapter 1 ended with new birth by the living word. Chapter 2 continues the picture: newborns need milk. First comes a list of things to throw off — malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander (v. 1). These are the sins that destroy the brotherly love Peter just commanded (1:22). Then comes the craving: “as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow” (v. 2). The word ‘pure’ (ἄδολος, without deceit) is the opposite of ‘deceit’ (δόλος) in verse 1. What you take in shapes what you become.

Then the image changes from a nursery to a building site. Believers come to Jesus, “a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious” (v. 4), and they themselves become “living stones” built into “a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood” (v. 5). Peter, whose name means ‘rock’, never claims to be the foundation; he gives that place to Christ alone, and calls every believer a stone. Paul uses the same picture: “in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).

The cornerstone divides people. For believers He is honour; for the disobedient He is “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense” (v. 8). The same Jesus who saves some causes others to stumble — not because He has failed, but because they refuse to obey the word. Jesus quoted Psalm 118 about Himself: “Did you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner’” (Matthew 21:42), and Peter quoted it to the very leaders who had rejected Him: He is “‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner’” (Acts 4:11).

sections.heading: The Identity of God's People
paragraphs: Verse 9 is one of the great identity statements of Scripture: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.” Every title was first given to Israel at Mount Sinai. Peter now gives them to a church made up largely of Gentiles. This is not because God has abandoned Israel, but because in Christ, Jews and Gentiles together form the people of God.

The point of the identity is mission. A priesthood exists to bring people to God and God to people. A royal priesthood represents the King. Believers are chosen not merely to enjoy God's favour but to “proclaim the excellence” of the One who rescued them. John saw the same in heaven: Christ “made us to be a Kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).

And the identity is pure grace. “who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (v. 10). Peter borrows Hosea's names for his children — ‘Not my people’ and ‘No mercy’ — and shows them reversed. If you feel like an outsider, unwanted or forgotten, this verse is God's answer: you have been named and claimed.

sections.heading: Living Well in a Hostile World
paragraphs: From verse 11 Peter turns to the believer's life among unbelievers. He reminds them again that they are “foreigners and pilgrims” (v. 11), and that the first battle is inside: “to abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.” Then he turns outward: “having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they see, glorify God in the day of visitation” (v. 12). This is Jesus' teaching: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

That includes respect for authority: “Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake” (v. 13). Remarkably, the king Peter tells them to honour was Nero, who would later execute Christians, possibly including Peter himself. Submission does not mean obeying commands to sin — Peter himself had said, ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29) — but it means respecting the role of government and living as good citizens, so that “by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men” (v. 15).

Verse 16 guards against two errors: believers are free, so they are not slaves to human institutions; but they are God's slaves, so their freedom is never a cover for sin. Verse 17 sums it up in four short commands: “Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.” Notice the careful balance: honour for everyone, including the emperor; love for the church; fear for God alone.

sections.heading: Following the Suffering Shepherd
paragraphs: Peter then speaks to household slaves, many of whom were believers serving unbelieving masters. He does not endorse slavery; he addresses slaves as moral agents with dignity before God and shows them how to live faithfully within an unjust situation. If they suffer for doing wrong, there is no credit in enduring it. “But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God” (v. 20). The principle reaches every believer who suffers unfairly — at work, at home or in society.

The reason is Christ: “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (v. 21). Peter had seen it with his own eyes. Jesus “did not sin” (v. 22), and when He was cursed, He “didn’t curse back” and did not threaten, “but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (v. 23). Jesus prayed for His executioners: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). The answer to injustice is not revenge but trust in the righteous Judge.

But Christ is more than an example. “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed” (v. 24). Peter is quoting Isaiah 53, the song of the Suffering Servant. To slaves who knew the whip, Peter says: your Lord was whipped too, and His wounds have healed your deepest wound. “For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (v. 25). Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

ntConnection.heading: The Cornerstone, the Priesthood and the Suffering Servant
paragraphs: The stone sayings of verses 6–8 appear across the New Testament. Paul combines the same two Isaiah passages: “even as it is written, ‘Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and no one who believes in him will be disappointed’” (Romans 9:33). He calls Christ “the chief cornerstone” of the church built “on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20). And Jesus' words to Peter stand behind it all: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly” (Matthew 16:18). Peter, the ‘rock’, now points away from himself to the true cornerstone.

The royal priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (vv. 5, 9) is the fulfilment of Hebrews' teaching: “Through him, then, let us offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name” (Hebrews 13:15). Paul calls the believer's whole life a sacrifice: “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). Every believer is a priest; every life is an altar.

Verses 22–25 are woven from Isaiah 53, the clearest Old Testament prophecy of Christ's atoning death. Peter quotes it not as a distant text but as an eyewitness of its fulfilment. The Gospels record the silence (Matthew 27:12), the beating (Mark 15:19) and the prayer for forgiveness (Luke 23:34). And the Shepherd who bore our sins is the Shepherd who said, “I am the good shepherd. I know my own, and I’m known by my own” (John 10:14).

lexicon.strongs: G3037 (rock πέτρα, pétra, G4073; cornerstone ἀκρογωνιαῖος, akrogōniaîos, G204)
lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a stone (literally or figuratively).” Peter uses λίθος five times in five verses: Christ the living stone, believers the living stones, the cornerstone of Isaiah 28, the rejected stone of Psalm 118, and the stumbling stone of Isaiah 8. The fisherman whom Jesus named Πέτρος, ‘rock’, and to whom He said ‘on this πέτρα I will build my assembly’, never claims the title for himself here. He gives the cornerstone to Christ and makes every believer a stone in the same house.

Strong's: “the priestly fraternity, i.e. sacerdotal order (figuratively).” ἱεράτευμα means a body or community of priests. In Israel only the descendants of Aaron could serve as priests. Peter says the whole church is a holy priesthood (v. 5) and a royal priesthood (v. 9) — echoing Exodus 19:6. Every believer has direct access to God through Christ and a priestly calling: to offer spiritual sacrifices and to represent God to the world.

Strong's: “an underwriting, i.e. copy for imitation (figuratively).” ὑπογραμμός was a schoolroom word: the line of letters a teacher wrote at the top of a child's tablet for the child to trace underneath. This is its only New Testament appearance. This study adds it to the pattern family beside τύπος (a model or imprint) and ὑπόδειγμα (an example). Christ's patient suffering is the line written at the top of your page. You follow it stroke by stroke, not by inventing your own letters.

Strong's: “to experience a sensation or impression (usually painful).” πάσχω is the key verb of 1 Peter, used twelve times, more than in any other New Testament letter. It means to undergo something done to you. Peter uses it both of Christ (v. 21, 23) and of believers (v. 19–20). This study gathers it with πάθημα (sufferings), συμπάσχω (suffer with Christ) and κακοπαθέω (endure hardship) into a new suffer family. Believers' suffering is never pointless when it is suffering with and for Christ.

Strong's: “a mole ("black eye") or blow-mark.” μώλωψ is the swollen bruise or welt left by a whip — the result of a flogging. Peter takes the word from Isaiah 53:5. To slaves who knew such marks on their own backs, he says that Christ bore them too, and that His wounds heal. ἰάομαι, from the heal family, is the physician's word. The primary healing is from sin, as the context shows; but the cross is also the ground of every healing God gives.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit is telling you who you are — and showing you how to live that identity before a watching world.

items.title: How Is Your Appetite?
items.body: The Spirit asks whether you are craving the word like a newborn craves milk. If your appetite is weak, it may be because something else is filling you — malice, envy, slander or other poisons of verse 1. Ask Him to show you what you need to put away, and to give you a fresh hunger for His word. “if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious” (v. 3), you were made for more.

items.title: You Belong
items.body: Do you feel rejected, overlooked or unwanted? Jesus was rejected by people but chosen and precious to God (v. 4). So are you. “who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people” (v. 10). The Spirit wants you to hear your names: chosen, royal, priestly, holy, God's own possession. Let that identity change how you walk into this week.

items.title: Who Are You Tempted to Curse Back?
items.body: Someone has treated you unfairly. The Spirit brings Jesus' example before you: “Who, when he was cursed, didn’t curse back. When he suffered, didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (v. 23). He is not asking you to pretend it does not hurt. He is asking you to hand the case to the righteous Judge. Who do you need to entrust to Him today?

audit.title: The Milk Check
audit.body: How much of God's word are you taking in each day compared with news, entertainment and social media (v. 2)? Which of the sins in verse 1 is spoiling your appetite?

audit.title: The Witness Check
audit.body: If your unbelieving neighbours, colleagues or family watched your conduct for a week, would they see good works that point to God (v. 12)? Where is your behaviour giving them reason to speak against you?

audit.title: The Retaliation Check
audit.body: When you are treated unfairly, do you insult back, threaten or plot revenge (v. 23)? How do you speak about authorities, bosses or leaders you disagree with (vv. 13–17)?

practices.title: Feed Like a Newborn
practices.body: For the next two weeks, set a fixed time each day — before your phone — to read one chapter of the New Testament slowly. Write one sentence about what it shows you of the Lord's goodness and one sentence about how you will obey it. Notice whether your appetite grows.

practices.title: Trace His Letters
practices.body: Write verse 23 on a card and carry it with you. The next time someone wrongs you, read it, pray it, and respond with a blessing instead of a curse. Then write the situation on the back of the card and pray, ‘Father, I commit this to You, the righteous Judge.’ Keep the card as a record of every time you followed His steps.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, I have tasted that You are gracious, and I want more of You. Help me put away all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander, and give me a newborn's hunger for the pure milk of Your word, so that I may grow. Thank You that You are the living stone, rejected by people but chosen and precious to God. Build me as a living stone into Your spiritual house, and make me a holy priest who offers spiritual sacrifices acceptable through You. Thank You that I am chosen, royal, holy and Your own possession. I was no people, and now I am Yours; I had no mercy, and now I have received mercy. Teach me to proclaim Your excellence. Help me abstain from desires that war against my soul and to live such a good life among unbelievers that they glorify God. Give me grace to honour all people, love Your family, fear God and honour those in authority. When I suffer unjustly, let me follow Your steps. You did not sin, You did not curse back, You did not threaten; You entrusted Yourself to the righteous Judge. Thank You that You bore my sins in Your body on the tree, and that by Your wounds I am healed. I was a wandering sheep; now I have returned to You, the Shepherd and Overseer of my soul. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Rejected Stone Before the Council
storyConnections.summary: After Peter and John healed a lame man at the temple, they were arrested and brought before the same council that had condemned Jesus. Filled with the Spirit, Peter declared that the man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised. Then he quoted Psalm 118 to their faces: Jesus is “‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner’” (Acts 4:11). The leaders were amazed, because Peter and John were ordinary, unschooled men, and “They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13). Years later Peter wrote the same truth to the scattered churches.

storyConnections.title: Jesus Silent Before His Accusers
storyConnections.summary: At His trial before the high priest, false witnesses lined up against Jesus, but “Jesus held his peace” (Matthew 26:63). They spat in His face and struck Him with their fists. Before Pilate, “When he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing” (Matthew 27:12), and “He gave him no answer, not even one word, so that the governor marveled greatly” (Matthew 27:14). Peter was in the courtyard that night, denying Him. Now he writes as an eyewitness of how Jesus suffered: no sin, no deceit, no curse, no threat — only trust in the One who judges righteously.

storyConnections.title: The Lost Sheep Brought Home
storyConnections.summary: Jesus told of a shepherd with a hundred sheep who lost one. He left the ninety-nine in the wilderness and searched until he found it, then laid it on his shoulders rejoicing and called his friends to celebrate. Jesus said there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who need no repentance. Peter knew what it was to stray; the Shepherd had found him by a charcoal fire and brought him home. So he writes, “For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (v. 25).
